# Brain Schema & Conventions

This file defines the entity types, YAML frontmatter standards, the page
standard, and naming conventions for this GBrain vault. `RESOLVER.md` decides
**where** a note goes; this file decides **how** it is shaped. Read both before
creating or editing any page.

## 1. Naming Conventions

- **All filenames are lower-case kebab-case**: `John Doe` → `john-doe.md`,
  `Atlas Dashboard` → `atlas-dashboard.md`.
- The filename slug is the **stable entity ID**. Cross-references use it.
- Disambiguate collisions with a qualifier suffix:
  `david-liu-greenlite.md`, `david-liu-meta.md`.
- Attachments for `foo.md` live in a sibling folder named exactly `foo/`
  (no `.md`), next to the file. Never a central attachments dump.
- Dates are ISO 8601 (`2026-01-15`). Meeting/journal slugs are date-prefixed:
  `2026-04-16-greenlite-workstream-sync.md`.

## 2. The Page Standard (compiled truth + timeline)

Every important entity page has two parts split by a horizontal rule:

```markdown
# Display Name

## Compiled Truth
<synthesized, always-current summary — rewritten when facts change>
- **State fields**: role, status, key context (2–4 bullets)
- **Open threads**: what is unresolved
- Cross-references: [[other-entity]]

---

## Timeline / Log
<append-only, reverse-chronological. Newest first. Never rewrite history.>
### 2026-04-16 — source: fathom
- what happened / what was decided
```

- **Top = "what is true now?"** Read it to get current state.
- **Bottom = "what happened?"** Append-only evidence log.
- Resolved open-threads migrate down into the timeline.

## 3. Source Attribution & Confidence

When a fact's provenance matters, annotate inline:
`(observed)`, `(self-described)`, `(inferred)`, `(reported: <source>)`.
Use `confidence: low|medium|high` in frontmatter for synthesized pages whose
Compiled Truth is uncertain.

## 4. Entity Frontmatter Schemas

All pages carry `type:`. `created`/`updated` are ISO dates. Empty multi-value
fields are `[]`. Wikilink references use the target slug: `[[first-last]]`.

**`name` vs `title` (important):** Entity types (`person`, `company`, `concept`,
`project`) are keyed by **`name`** (title-case) — **do NOT add a `title:` key to
an entity page.** `title` is reserved for note/document types (`meeting`,
`source`, `reflection`), where it holds the human-readable, *non-slugified*
display title. For an entity, the slugified identity already lives in the
filename and the H1 heading (`# first-last`); a **job title** goes in `role:`;
an **ASCII / de-accented spelling** of the name goes in `aliases:` (e.g. name
`Doğan Gülcan` → alias `Dogan Gulcan`).

### person — `people/first-last.md`
```yaml
type: person
name: First Last       # title-case; entities use `name`, never a `title:` key
aliases: ["Firstname", "email@example.com", "@handle"]  # incl. ASCII spelling of accented names
company: <company-slug>
role: ""               # job title, e.g. "CTO" — NOT a `title:` key
status: active | former | candidate | prospect | contact
relationship: coworker | report | manager | candidate | recruiter | vendor | mentor
linkedin: ""
github: ""
email: ""
tags: []
created: <date>
updated: <date>
```

161	## Former Colleagues (Aetion)
162	...
163	## Former Colleagues (Squarespace)
164	...
165	```
166	
167	This would dramatically improve graph connectivity and make people-centric queries faster.
168	
169	---
170	
171	## 3. Frontmatter and Tagging Strategy
172	
173	### 3a. The Tag Gap Is Your Biggest Findability Problem
174	
175	Only 7% of files have frontmatter tags. This means search is almost entirely dependent on full-text search and directory structure. For a 2,485-file vault, that's a significant findability bottleneck.
176	
177	**Recommended minimum tagging taxonomy:**
178	
179	```yaml
180	# Content type tags
181	tags:
182	  - type/meeting       # 1:1s, syncs, standups
183	  - type/decision      # Decisions made
184	  - type/reference     # Evergreen reference material
185	  - type/interview     # Candidate interviews
186	  - type/learning      # Course notes, book notes
187	  - type/planning      # Roadmaps, goals, OKRs
188	  - type/retrospective # Retros, postmortems
189	  - type/clipping      # Saved articles
190	
191	# Domain tags
192	  - domain/ai          # AI/ML topics
193	  - domain/leadership  # Management, coaching
194	  - domain/engineering  # Technical topics
195	  - domain/recruiting  # Hiring pipeline
196	  - domain/product     # Product decisions
197	
198	# Status tags (for living documents)
199	  - status/active
200	  - status/archived
201	  - status/draft
202	```
203	
204	You don't need to retroactively tag all 2,485 files. Start with a rule: every new note gets at least one `type/` tag and one `domain/` tag. Then progressively backfill high-value directories like `greenlite/people/` and `greenlite/planning/`.
205	
206	### 3b. Standardize People Note Frontmatter
207	
208	Your people notes have no consistent frontmatter. Adding structured metadata would enable powerful queries:
209	
210	```yaml
211	---
212	tags:
213	  - type/person
214	role: Senior Engineer
215	team: ML Platform
216	start-date: 2024-03
217	reports-to: Edward Bridges
218	status: active    # active | departed | candidate
219	---
220	```
221	
222	This would let AI tools answer questions like "who is on the ML team?" or "show me all 1:1 notes for active reports" without full-text scanning.
223	
224	### 3c. Add Frontmatter to Journal Entries
225	
226	Your daily notes have a `creation date` field but nothing else. Adding a few structured fields would improve temporal queries:
227	
228	```yaml
229	---
230	creation date: 2026-02-10 10:43
231	type: daily-note
232	week: 2026-W07
233	highlights:
234	  - 1:1 with Paul Lee
235	  - Detection working session
236	---
237	```
238	
239	The `highlights` field is particularly valuable — it gives AI tools a quick index of what happened each day without parsing the full note.
240	
241	---
242	
243	## 4. Interlinking Recommendations
244	
245	### 4a. The Personal Section Is an Island
246	
247	With only 0.1 links per file, `personal/` is almost entirely disconnected from the rest of the vault. This is the biggest graph connectivity gap. Some natural link opportunities:
248	
249	- **Reading notes → Work topics:** If you read "AI Engineering" by Chip Huyen, that note should link to `work/greenlite/ai-planning/` and `personal/development/machine-learning/`. Currently these are isolated.
250	- **Development notes → Work application:** Your leadership development notes should link to the people you're applying those techniques with.
251	- **Health notes → Journal entries:** When health events affect work schedule, cross-linking provides context.
252	
253	### 4b. Journal Entries Are Well-Linked but One-Directional
254	
255	Your journal entries link out to people, plans, and projects — that's excellent. But the target notes rarely link back. This creates a "spoke" pattern where the journal is a hub but other notes are leaves.
256	
257	**Recommendation:** At the bottom of key reference notes (people files, project docs, planning docs), add a "Related Journal Entries" section or use Obsidian's backlinks pane more actively. Even a simple `## Log` section at the bottom of people files that links back to specific journal dates would create bidirectional connections.
258	
259	### 4c. Create Topic MOCs (Maps of Content)
260	
261	Your vault would benefit enormously from 5-10 MOC notes that act as navigation hubs. Suggested MOCs:
262	
263	| MOC | Location | Purpose |
264	|-----|----------|---------|
265	| `work/greenlite/00-greenlite-overview.md` | Current work hub | Links to all active projects, people, planning docs |
266	| `work/interview-prep/00-prep-overview.md` | Interview prep hub | Links to all prep materials by category |
267	| `personal/development/00-learning-map.md` | Learning hub | Links all courses, books, topics with status |
268	| `personal/reading/00-reading-list.md` | Reading hub | Links all book notes with brief status/rating |
269	| `work/experience/00-story-bank.md` | STAR stories hub | Index of all behavioral/technical stories |
270	
271	Prefix with `00-` so they sort to the top of each directory.
272	
273	### 4d. Cross-Link Experience Stories to Source Projects
274	
275	Your `work/experience/` directory (53 files, only 5 with wikilinks) is a goldmine of STAR stories, but they're disconnected from the source material. Each story about a Greenlite project should link to the relevant project note, people involved, and journal entries where the work happened. This makes the stories findable from multiple angles and helps keep them updated.
276	
277	### 4e. Link Clippings to Where You Use Them
278	
279	Your Clippings are well-tagged (30 of 32 have frontmatter tags) and have decent link density. But they're mostly self-contained. When a clipping informs a work decision or a learning note, add a wikilink in both directions. For example, the "Measuring Engineering Organizations" clipping should link to `work/greenlite/engineering/Engineering metrics/`.
280	
281	---
282	
283	## 5. Templates
284	
285	### 5a. You Need More Templates
286	
287	Five templates for a 2,485-file vault is quite lean. Consider adding:
288	
289	| Template | Purpose |
290	|----------|---------|
291	| `person-template.md` | Standardized frontmatter + sections for people notes |
292	| `project-template.md` | Status, goals, stakeholders, decisions, links |
293	| `book-note-template.md` | Metadata, key takeaways, application notes, links to related work |
294	| `clipping-template.md` | Source, date, tags, summary, application |
295	| `1-on-1-template.md` | Date, agenda, action items, follow-ups (for appending to people files) |
296	| `decision-record-template.md` | Context, options considered, decision, rationale |
297	
298	### 5b. The Daily Note Template Could Be Richer
299	
300	Your current template has Agenda, Open Tasks, and Reading sections. Consider adding:
301	
302	```markdown
303	## Decisions Made
304	
305	## Follow-ups from Today
306	- [ ]
307	
308	## Links to Relevant Notes
309	
310	```
311	
312	The "Decisions Made" section is particularly valuable for AI retrieval — it gives a clear signal of what was decided vs. merely discussed.
313	
314	---
315	
316	## 6. Quick Wins (Low Effort, High Impact)
317	
318	1. **Rehome the 4 root orphan files** — 5 minutes, cleaner vault root
319	2. **Add the "About the Author" block to CLAUDE.md** — 2 minutes, dramatically better AI context
320	3. **Add `type/person` tag to all people files** — 30 minutes, enables people-centric queries
321	4. **Create a Greenlite overview MOC** — 15 minutes, becomes your daily launch pad
322	5. **Add "Sensitive Areas" to CLAUDE.md** — 2 minutes, protects private content from AI surfacing
323	
324	---
325	
326	## 7. What's Already Working Well
327	
328	To be clear, the vault has significant strengths worth preserving:
329	
330	- **Journal linking is excellent.** Your daily notes actively link to people, projects, and plans. This is the backbone of your graph.
331	- **The `work/greenlite/` structure is well-organized.** Clean separation of people, interviews, engineering, planning, and projects.
332	- **Fathom recording links in people notes** create a reliable audit trail for 1:1 conversations.
333	- **The CLAUDE.md file exists at all** and includes QMD collection mappings — most vaults don't have this, and it's a real advantage for AI-assisted search.
334	- **Consistent journal naming** (`<date>-Day.md`) makes temporal navigation reliable.
335	- **The `work/experience/` STAR story bank** is a genuinely useful career asset that most people don't build.
336	
337	---
338	
339	## Suggested Priority Order
340	
341	1. CLAUDE.md improvements (sections 1a-1d) — immediate, no structural changes
342	2. Root orphan cleanup (2a) — quick win
343	3. Frontmatter tagging for new notes going forward (3a) — habit change
344	4. People note frontmatter standardization (3b) — high value for queries
345	5. Topic MOCs (4c) — creates navigation hubs
346	6. Directory naming standardization (2b) — can do incrementally
347	7. Cross-linking personal → work (4a, 4d, 4e) — ongoing improvement
348	8. Additional templates (5a-5b) — supports all of the above

2	title: Modeling Entity Documents (Compiled Truth / Timeline) in wakil
3	status: draft
4	audience: wakil design
5	---
6	
7	# Modeling Entity Documents in wakil
8	
9	`wakil`'s target knowledge base uses a two-part convention for important
10	entity pages — people, companies — inherited from GBrain and documented in
11	the target vault's own `schema.md`: a **Compiled Truth** section holding
12	synthesized current state, and a **Timeline / Log** holding an append-only,
13	reverse-chronological evidence record. `wakil/PROMPT.md` already commits to
14	preserving this split, but nothing in the codebase implements it yet:
15	`Note`/`Memory`/`Relationship` exist in `storage/schema.py`, but there is no
16	notion of a Timeline entry, no Open Threads lifecycle, and no command that
17	touches a Compiled Truth section.
18	
19	This spec starts from a critical read of how the pattern is actually used in
20	a real, long-running vault, then proposes a concrete model — what belongs in
21	the Markdown, what belongs in SQLite, and how content moves between them —
22	that fills the gap without importing the large autonomous system GBrain uses
23	to back the same visible format.
24	
25	## What the pattern looks like in practice
26	
27	Sampled directly from a real vault's `companies/` and `people/` documents,
28	against the documented spec in that vault's `schema.md` §2 ("The Page
29	Standard: compiled truth + timeline").
30	
31	1. **Compiled Truth is empty for most of the vault.** The large majority of
32	   sampled pages carry only the placeholder text (`_Synthesized current
33	   state — rewrite when facts change._`) with zero real content, and well
34	   over a hundred lines of raw, unsynthesized interview notes dumped into
35	   Timeline instead. The synthesis step the format promises has not run for
36	   most entities — the two-part structure is aspirational, not actual, for
37	   most of the vault.
38	
39	2. **Backlinks are baked into Timeline text**, e.g. `- **2026-06-04** |
40	   Referenced in ['2024 06 12 Wed'](journal/...)`. These are derived graph
41	   metadata, not evidence of what happened, and they directly contradict the
42	   vault's own definition of Timeline as an "append-only evidence log." This
43	   causes two concrete problems: the file changes every time something
44	   merely *references* it — churn unrelated to the entity's own history —
45	   and it interleaves mechanical noise with real chronological content,
46	   sometimes literally ahead of the real entries in file order.
47	
48	3. **Open Threads drifted from its documented shape.** The vault's own
49	   `schema.md` defines Open Threads as an inline bullet inside Compiled
50	   Truth (`- **Open threads**: what is unresolved`). Real files that use it
51	   instead give it its own `## Open Threads` H2. The convention as practiced
52	   differs from the convention as written, with nothing flagging the drift.
53	
54	4. **Provenance is carried as hand-written prose tags** —
55	   `[Source: [[sources/...]], 2026-06-23]` — with no structured backing. It
56	   works as long as a human maintains it carefully, but it's unqueryable
57	   ("what do we know about X sourced only from meeting Y?") and easy to lose
58	   silently on a hand edit, since nothing checks that a claim's citation
59	   survives a rewrite.
60	
61	5. **The simplicity of the visible format hides a large system.** In GBrain
62	   (inspected via its code graph), Compiled Truth and Timeline are thin views
63	   over a `pages` table (`compiled_truth`, `timeline` TEXT columns, plus a
64	   generation counter for cache invalidation), a `page_versions` snapshot
65	   table, a structured `timeline_entries` table
66	   (`page_id, date, source, summary, detail`), a `links` graph table,
67	   `content_chunks` with synthesis-boosted search ranking, silent
68	   `stubEntityPage` auto-creation for referenced-but-undocumented entities,
69	   and a fact/atom extraction pipeline with contradiction detection feeding
70	   synthesis. That is a large, partly-autonomous system — exactly what
71	   `wakil/CLAUDE.md` rules out ("large agent frameworks," "hidden background
72	   behavior," "automatic rewriting without review," "opaque memory
73	   systems"). The markdown pattern is worth keeping; the machinery GBrain
74	   uses to back it is not something to port wholesale.
75	
76	**Bottom line:** the format is sound and worth preserving, but a real vault
77	run this way for a while shows what happens when the promotion step (raw →
78	synthesized) has no tooling: content piles up in the append-only half and the
79	"what's true now" half rots. That's the gap `wakil` needs to fill —
80	deliberately, with human confirmation at the point of synthesis, not by
81	copying GBrain's autonomous pipeline.
82	
83	## Markdown shape (source of truth, unchanged in spirit)
84	
85	```markdown
86	# Display Name
87	
88	## Compiled Truth
89	<synthesized, always-current summary>
90	- state-field bullets
91	
92	## Open Threads
93	- unresolved items, each citing its source
94	
95	---
96	
97	## Timeline / Log
98	### 2026-04-16 — [Source: [[sources/...|label]]]
99	- what happened
100	```
101	
102	- **Open Threads gets its own H2** — codifying what real files already do in
103	  practice, and giving `wakil` a stable H2→H2 parse boundary instead of
104	  scraping mixed-purpose bullets out of prose.
105	- **No backlink text in Timeline, ever.** `wakil`'s writer never emits
106	  "Referenced in" lines; backlinks are a query, not stored prose (see
107	  below). `wakil`'s indexer recognizes legacy backlink lines as noise
108	  (`^- .*\| Referenced in`) and offers their removal as part of a reviewable
109	  diff during synthesis — never stripped silently.
110	- Timeline citations standardize on `[Source: [[wikilink|label]]]` — already
111	  the pattern in the better-written pages — over a bare `source: fathom`
112	  label, since a wikilink is resolvable and a plain label isn't.
113	- No new frontmatter marker is needed to identify an entity page:
114	  `type: person|company|...` already says so, and `Note` indexing already
115	  captures frontmatter.
116	
117	Because the target vault is external to `wakil`, this shape is a proposed
118	amendment to that vault's own `schema.md`, reviewed and merged there like any
119	other change — not a `wakil`-only convention enforced silently.
120	
121	## What lives in SQLite, and why
122	
123	`wakil` extends its existing `Note`/`Memory`/`Relationship` tables rather
124	than adding a parallel schema. Each choice below is checked against the
125	project's own bar: *does this clearly improve local knowledge work for one
126	user?*
127	
128	| Data | Verdict |
129	|---|---|
130	| **Compiled Truth content** | Not stored in SQLite. Markdown only — git already provides full version/diff/revert history, which is exactly what a GBrain-style `page_versions` table would duplicate. |
131	| **Open Threads items** | Existing `Memory` rows, `memory_type='question'` (already named as an example Memory type), `note_id` = the entity's `Note`. Resolution is a `state` transition plus a `Relationship(predicate='resolves')` edge — the "resolved open-threads migrate down into the timeline" rule, with zero new schema. |
132	| **Timeline entries** | Existing `Memory` rows, `memory_type='event'` (a new value on the already free-string column — no migration), `note_id` = entity `Note`, `source_id` = originating `Source`. **One genuine new column: `Memory.event_date` (nullable date).** `created_at` records when the SQLite row was written, not when the dated event happened, and Timeline ordering needs the latter. |
133	| **A dedicated `timeline_entries` table (GBrain-style)** | Rejected. Its only advantage over `SELECT * FROM memories WHERE note_id=X AND memory_type='event' ORDER BY event_date` is a marginally cleaner query, at the cost of forking the whole Memory lifecycle (state, promotion, dedup) into a second, unmaintained path. |
134	| **Backlinks / graph edges** | Existing `Relationship` table, widened with two new nullable columns, `subject_note_id` and `object_note_id` (mirrors the nullable-provenance pattern the table already uses for `source_id`/`note_id`). Wikilinks are Note↔Note structural edges, not Memory↔Memory semantic ones — today's `Relationship` only models the latter. Backlinks become a live query (`WHERE object_note_id = X`) — the actual fix for the baked-in-text anti-pattern above, not just a ban on the symptom. |
135	| **Search-ranking boost for synthesized content (GBrain's `chunk_source`)** | Not now — solves a chunked/hybrid-search problem `wakil` doesn't have yet; revisit only if a chunking/embedding layer lands. |
136	
137	## Write / promotion path — no autonomous rewriting anywhere
138	
139	Every step is propose → diff → confirm, reusing the two-phase
140	`prepare_ingest` / `apply_ingest` plus `IngestProposal` / `ProposedFile`
141	shape already implemented in `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`.
142	
143	1. **Ingest** (implemented today): raw source → candidate `Memory` rows.
144	   Extraction is extended to tag date-bearing, entity-linked content as
145	   `memory_type='event'` with `event_date` set and `note_id` resolved
146	   through the existing related-note search / resolver routing.
147	2. **Review/promote** (Phase 5, not yet built): `wakil memory promote <id>`
148	   moves a memory to durable — no special-casing for `event`/`question`
149	   types, same command, same review queue.
150	3. **Timeline append**: once a durable `event` memory has a `note_id`,
151	   `wakil` proposes appending a `### <event_date> — [Source: ...]` block to
152	   that note's Timeline as an explicit confirmable step during promotion
153	   ("append to `<slug>` Timeline? [y/N]") — never folded in silently.
154	4. **Compiled Truth synthesis — new command `wakil entity compile <slug>`**:
155	   - Resolve `<slug>` → `Note`, verify frontmatter `type` is an entity type.
156	   - Pull all durable `Memory` rows tied to that `note_id`.
157	   - The model drafts a rewritten Compiled Truth + Open Threads block
158	     only — Timeline is never touched by this command.
159	   - Render as a colorized diff of just that section (a surgical replace,
160	     not a whole-file overwrite), reusing the existing diff-preview UI.
161	   - On confirm: write, commit as `wakil note: recompile <slug> compiled
162	     truth`, logged via `GitChange` (`operation="entity_compile"`) rather
163	     than `IngestRun`, which is source-shaped and doesn't fit a
164	     no-source operation.
165	   - The same pass proposes moving any now-resolved Open Thread down into a
166	     one-line Timeline entry, shown in the same diff.
167	   - This is the concrete, entity-scoped version of `docs/memory-model.md`'s
168	     abstract "reconsolidation as a reviewable proposal."
169	
170	## Entity auto-stubbing
171	
172	`wakil` does not replicate GBrain's silent `stubEntityPage`. New-file
173	creation is exactly the durable-Markdown change that must stay reviewable.
174	Instead, the existing ingest preview is extended: when relationship
175	extraction finds a mentioned entity with no matching `Note`, it's added to
176	the `IngestProposal` as `stub_entities: list[ProposedFile]`, pre-filled via
177	the same resolver-driven routing already used for proposed notes, shown in
178	the same diff, and created only on confirmation. For ingests that mention
179	many people (e.g. a transcript), the default is one summary confirmation
180	("create N stub pages? [y/N]") rather than N separate diffs.
181	
182	## Deviations from existing docs — flagged, not silent
183	
184	- **Memory state vocabulary**: this model is written against `PROMPT.md`'s
185	  implemented states (`working/candidate/durable/archived/rejected`,
186	  matching `storage/schema.py`), not `docs/memory-model.md`'s proposed
187	  `candidate/active/dormant/archived` plus `strength/activation/
188	  support_count` model. The Timeline/Open-Threads-as-Memory mapping is
189	  orthogonal to which vocabulary wins; reconciling the two is a separate,
190	  still-open decision.
191	- **New `memory_type='event'`** — not in `PROMPT.md`'s example list, but
192	  backward-compatible since the column is a free string.
193	- **New `Memory.event_date` column** — a genuine addition beyond
194	  `PROMPT.md`'s field list; justified above.
195	- **New `Relationship.subject_note_id` / `object_note_id`** — a genuine
196	  addition; today's `Relationship` is Memory-only.
197	- **Explicitly rejected from GBrain**: `page_versions` (redundant with git),
198	  `timeline_entries` (redundant with `Memory`), `links` (redundant with a
199	  widened `Relationship`), `chunk_source` boosting (no chunking layer yet),
200	  silent `stubEntityPage` auto-creation (violates confirm-before-write), and
201	  the whole fact/atom/contradiction/dream-cycle autonomous pipeline (out of
202	  scope, and in conflict with `wakil`'s report-only `dream` command).
203	
204	## Where this lands in `TODO.md`
205	
206	This is new design surface. It extends **Phase 5: Memory Lifecycle**
207	(currently empty) with the entity-specific pieces above, and adds one item
208	under the existing "Wikilink/tag extraction during indexing" TODO to also
209	populate `Relationship.subject_note_id` / `object_note_id`.
210	
211	## Critical files
212	
213	- `src/wakil/storage/schema.py` — `Memory` / `Relationship` extensions
214	  (`event_date`, `subject_note_id`, `object_note_id`)
215	- `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py` — extend `prepare_ingest` /
216	  `apply_ingest` and `ProposedFile` / `IngestProposal` for `stub_entities`
217	  and Timeline-append proposals
218	- `src/wakil/app/workspace_service.py` — wikilink/backlink indexing
219	  (existing TODO item)
220	- new `src/wakil/app/entity_service.py` (or similar) — `entity compile`
221	  command logic
222	- target vault's `schema.md` — proposed amendment (Open Threads as H2, no
223	  backlink text in Timeline, wikilink-style Timeline citations), reviewed as
224	  a change to that vault, not to `wakil`
225

status: draft
audience: wakil design

# Entity Resolution and Routing

`docs/entity-model.md` covers **shape**: what a Compiled Truth / Timeline page
looks like once it exists. This doc covers **place**: which of the ~20
top-level directories in the target vault a given piece of raw knowledge
should land in before it can be shaped at all. The target vault's own
`RESOLVER.md` is a worked example of this problem — a priority-ordered
decision list that claims to be "the single authority for *where* knowledge
lands." This is a critical read of that document against how the vault it
governs actually looks on disk, with an eye toward what `wakil`'s own
resolver logic (`ingest_service.py`'s "existing related-note search /
resolver routing," referenced but not yet specified in `entity-model.md`)
should and shouldn't copy.

## The mechanism, as written

`RESOLVER.md` is a ten-rule waterfall, evaluated top to bottom, first match
wins:

| # | Test | Destination |
|---|------|-------------|
| 1 | Sensitive (review, feedback, compensation) | `sensitive/` — **stop** |
| 2 | Person | `people/first-last.md` |
| 3 | Company / employer / vendor / client | `companies/<slug>.md` |
| 4 | Meeting / transcript / session note | `meetings/` (synthesized) or `sources/` (raw) |
| 5 | Project (owned, dated, deliverable) | `projects/<scope>/<slug>.md` |
| 6 | Concept (reusable, instructional, timeless) | `concepts/<slug>.md` |
| 7 | Idea (generative output, proposal, writing) | `ideas/<slug>.md` |
| 8 | Career / org structure (ladders, STAR stories) | `organization/<slug>.md` |
| 9 | Dated work log | `journal/YYYY/...` |
| 10 | Otherwise | `archive/` (historical) or `inbox/` (unresolved) |

Two things are layered on top of the waterfall: a dedicated **"hard call"**
section that disambiguates rule 5 vs. rule 6 with a worked test (owner/due
date vs. none) and a `split` verb for content that is genuinely both; and a
**linking rule** (absolute vault-root paths only, never relative) that keeps
cross-references stable when a file moves or is split. `schema.md` then picks
up where `RESOLVER.md` stops, defining the YAML frontmatter and page shape
for each destination.

## What works

- **Priority ordering resolves the one conflict it was built for.** A
  performance review *about* a person still hits rule 1 before rule 2, so
  sensitive content never has a chance to land in a personal file that gets
  casually surfaced. That's the right design for the one ambiguity the
  document was clearly written around.
- **The concept/project split is a real disambiguation, not just a
  definition.** It gives an owner/due-date test *and* an escape hatch
  (`split`) for mixed content, rather than forcing a false binary. This is
  the one pair the document treats with the rigor the whole taxonomy needs.
- **"Exactly one canonical file" plus absolute linking is a coherent pair.**
  Because links never encode a relative path, a file can be moved or split

authoritative. A router that's silent on half its own vault isn't wrong so
much as it's overclaiming: "single authority" should mean the decision list
is exhaustive, or the claim should be softened to "authority for entity-type
content," which is what it actually is.

**Reflection's current destination is the problem, not just an undocumented
one.** `schema.md` fully specifies `type: reflection` →
`wiki/personal/reflections/**`, and sampled files confirm it's used exactly
as documented (`wiki/personal/reflections/2026-05-30-infrastructure-for-thinking.md`
carries `type: reflection`, `date: 2026-05-30`, `week: 2026-W22`). But that
destination sits in `wiki/` — a directory `RESOLVER.md` never mentions
(finding #5's blind spot) and one with no structural relationship to
`ideas/`, even though a reflection and an idea are the same kind of thing by
provenance: both self-generated, both produced rather than consumed. Adding
a resolver rule that still points at `wiki/personal/reflections/` (the
earlier version of this section) would close the routing gap but leave
produced knowledge scattered across two unrelated top-level directories for
no reason other than history.

The better fix is structural: make `ideas/` the vault's operational home for
*all* produced knowledge, and nest reflection under it —
`ideas/reflections/YYYY-MM-DD-slug.md` — alongside the existing flat
`ideas/<slug>.md` proposal files, rather than leaving reflection in `wiki/`
at all. This is consistent with how `ideas/` already handles variation
within itself: it doesn't split by domain via subdirectories, it uses `tags`
(`business-ideas`, `writing`, `job-search`) — so a `reflections/` subfolder
for the one shape of idea content that's dated and needs its own chronology
(mirroring `journal/YYYY/`) is a small, consistent extension, not a new
pattern. `RESOLVER.md` rule 7 becomes a single "is this produced (self-
generated) knowledge?" test with a shape-based sub-route: dated, first-
person, processing → `ideas/reflections/`; generative, proposing → flat
`ideas/<slug>.md`. `schema.md` would need its `reflection` destination
updated to match.

recommendation implies moving ~22 existing files (plus `index.md`) out of
`wiki/personal/reflections/` into `ideas/reflections/`, not just adding a
line to `RESOLVER.md`. That's a real migration with real link-rewrite work
(every `[[wiki/personal/reflections/...]]` reference updates), which is why
it belongs in a "recommendation" section rather than being treated as
free. It's still the correct end state — the alternative is a resolver rule
that's internally consistent but permanently papers over a location that
contradicts the taxonomy it's supposed to express.

The candidate fix the user floated first — `sources/reflections/`, on the
reasoning that a reflection is "another source of inputs" — still doesn't
hold up, for the same reason as before: every value in `schema.md`'s
`origin` enum (`transcript | article | twitter | export | manual`) describes
an *externally captured* channel, confirmed by a sampled file
(`sources/ai-resources.md`, `origin: manual`, a list of external links).
`sources/` protects one clean signal — externally-originated raw material —
and a reflection's provenance is the opposite: self-generated, and often
already a finished thought rather than raw material (the sampled file ends
"Whether this is the right investment of time or a form of productive
procrastination is genuinely open. Probably some of both" — that's
synthesis, not a transcript). `ideas/reflections/`, not `sources/
reflections/`, is where the provenance signal actually points.

Two smaller things surfaced while sampling reflection files, flagged but not
resolved here: they use a bare `## Compiled Truth` header with no Timeline,
despite being one-shot dated entries rather than accumulating entity pages —
a shape mismatch for `entity-model.md` to pick up, not `RESOLVER.md`; and
`reflections/index.md` uses `type: index`, a tenth frontmatter type never
enumerated in `schema.md` §4 — the same "usage outruns documented schema"
pattern as finding #1, just for a different type. Both travel with the files
if/when they move to `ideas/reflections/`.

        f"origin: {json.dumps(proposal.origin)}",
        f"title: {json.dumps(proposal.title)}",
        f"retrieved: {date}",
        "---",
        "",

    return ProposedFile(path=str(path), content="\n".join(frontmatter_lines) + proposal.text + "\n")

title: Entity Metadata — A Critical Read of schema.md §4
status: draft
audience: wakil design

# Entity Metadata

`docs/entity-resolution.md` covered **where** knowledge lands (`RESOLVER.md`).
`docs/entity-model.md` covered the **Compiled Truth / Timeline** shape of an
important page. This doc covers what's left: **`schema.md` §4, "Entity
Frontmatter Schemas"** — the YAML contract each entity type is supposed to
carry — audited against how ~2,500 real files in the target vault actually
use it. Where the earlier docs sampled a handful of files per finding, this
one censuses whole categories (every `person` file, every `company` file,
etc.) so the claims below are counts, not impressions.

## The vault doesn't have 9 types — it has ~30

`schema.md` §4 documents nine: `person`, `company`, `project`, `meeting`,
`concept`, `source`, `journal`, `assessment`, `reflection`. A vault-wide
census of `type:` frontmatter values turns up considerably more:

| Type | Count | Documented? |
|---|---|---|
| `journal` | 939 | yes |
| `person` | 430 | yes |
| `concept` | 392 | yes (282 physically in `concepts/` — see below) |
| `company` | 260 | yes |
| `project` | 224 | yes |
| **`learning-agenda`** | **151** | **no** |
| `source` (+ `"source"` quoted) | 127 + 29 | yes |
| `meeting` | 63 | yes |
| `assessment` | 28 | yes |
| `reflection` | 26 | yes |
| `idea` | 12 | no (routing rule exists in `RESOLVER.md`, no schema) |
| `meta` | 8 | no |
| `report`, `article` | 5, 4 | no |
| `documentation` | 3 | no |
| `transcript`, `research`, `procedure` | 2 each | no |
| `organization`, `index`, `decision`, `daily-note`, `convention`, `workstream`, `working-session`, `project-draft`, `original`, `observation`, `encounter` | 1 each | `organization` has a routing rule, no schema; rest undocumented |

Two of these are not noise. `learning-agenda` (151 files, structured
day-by-day curricula under `learning-agendas/<curriculum>/day-NN-<topic>/`)
is bigger than `meeting`, `assessment`, and `reflection` combined, and
`schema.md` and `RESOLVER.md` are both silent on it. `organization` — the
type `RESOLVER.md` rule 8 routes to — is used as a literal `type:` value
exactly once; the other ~104 files in `organization/` declare `type:
concept` instead (see below). The `concept` row's discrepancy (392 vault-wide
vs. 282 in `concepts/`) is explained almost entirely by this: `organization/`
borrowing `concept`'s schema wholesale is not a one-off, it's most of the
gap.

## Per-type audit: documented schema vs. real usage

For each documented type, the table below gives the schema's declared fields
against the field actually observed in every file of that type, with the
count and percentage where it's informative.

### `person` (`people/*.md`, 430 files)

Core fields (`name`, `type`, `company`, `status`, `tags`, `role`,
`relationship`, `linkedin`, `aliases`, `email`, `github`) sit at 86–99%
adherence — the best-conforming identity type in the vault. Undocumented
fields in real use: `end-date` (109 files, 25%), `linkedin-link` (14, a
duplicate of `linkedin`), `team` (10), `link` (8), `level` (8), `last_name`/
`first_name` (8 each, competing with `name`), `title` (7 — a direct
violation of §4's own rule, see below), `linear_id` (7, a Linear
integration), `confidence` (7, correctly used per §3), `start_date`/
`location`/`_migrated_sources` (≤6 each).

### `company` (`companies/*.md`, 256 files)

Also strong: `category` (251, 98%), `aliases` (225, 88%), `website`/`stage`
(219 each), `key-people`/`industry` (218 each), `interview-dates` (215, 84%).
The interesting drift here is contamination, not extension: 4 files each
carry `role`, `relationship`, `linkedin`, `github`, `email` — person
schema fields on a company page, almost certainly a migration script
applying the wrong template to a handful of files.

### `project` (`projects/**/*.md`, 220 files)

**Every single project file (220/220) carries `title:`, and 219 also carry
`name:`.** §4 states explicitly that entity types "do NOT add a `title:` key
to an entity page." For `project`, that rule is violated at 100% — not a
handful of stragglers, the entire category. Also present and undocumented:
`year`/`week`/`day`/`date` (37 files — date-anchored, journal-shaped
sub-entries), `pillar` (17), and a `product_lead`/`layer`/`engineering`/
`design`/`customer_sponsors` cluster (9 files each — reads like one
specific team's RACI convention, not a vault-wide one).

### `concept` (`concepts/*.md`, 282 files)

Same story as `project`: `title:` appears on 277/282 files (98%), against
280 `name:` — the rule is violated almost universally here too. Also:
`status`/`end-date`/`company` (17 files each) and `workstream` (14) —
project-shaped fields on concept pages, which is either schema bleed or (per
`docs/entity-resolution.md`'s concept/project "hard call") content that was
never run through that disambiguation and is sitting in the wrong place.
`kindle-sync` (8 files) is a small, real Readwise/Kindle integration field.

### `meeting` (`meetings/*.md`, 62 files)

The highest-adherence type: `title`/`date`/`attendees` at 100%, `tags`/
`company` at 98%, `transcript`/`source`/`project`/`decisions`/`action-items`
at 94%. But `created` (50, 81%) and `updated` (21, 34%) are used constantly
despite not being in §4's `meeting` block at all, and — more importantly —
20 files carry `stage` and 18 carry `status`. This is very likely already an
informal implementation of the exact "when does a `sources/` transcript
count as synthesized" threshold `docs/entity-resolution.md` finding #9
flagged as undefined. It should be formalized, not invented from scratch.

### `journal` (`journal/**/*.md`, 939 files, 300 sampled)

Fully consistent across the sample: `year`, `week`, `type`, `topics`,
`title`, `tags`, `people`, `day`, `date`, `created` all at 300/300 — despite
`year`, `day`, `title`, `created`, and `topics` not appearing in §4's
`journal` block at all. This is the inverse of the drift seen elsewhere: real
practice is *more* complete and *more* consistent than the documentation.
`workstream`/`status`/`company` (43 files, 14%) mark entries that are
entirely about one project — a legitimate, minority-case extension.

### `source` (`sources/**/*.md`, 135 files)

The most field-diverse type in the vault by a wide margin — over 20 distinct
field names in use against a 5-field documented schema. Beyond the
documented `title`/`origin`/`url`/`captured`/`tags`: `created` (117, distinct
from `captured`), `published` (67, a *third* date — when the source itself
was published, vs. when it was captured), `source` (44 — a field literally
named `source` inside a `type: source` file), `company` (40), `description`
(37), `authors`/`author` (35/34, plural and singular coexisting), `link` (33,
duplicating `url`), `recording_url` (28), `readwise_updated`/`readwise_id`
(26 each, a Readwise integration). This isn't disorganized so much as
under-modeled: raw material genuinely has different natural metadata
depending on where it came from (a book highlight, a recorded meeting, a
tweet), and §4 already has exactly one precedent for handling that —
the optional `sources/messages/**` email-thread block — it just wasn't
extended to the other origins that clearly need it.

### `assessment` (`sensitive/**/*.md`, 27 files)

Perfect adherence on the documented fields (27/27 across `subject`,
`period`, `sensitive`, `tags`, `created`). But `company`, `workstream`, and
`status` each appear on 26/27 files (96%) and `end-date` on 25/27 (93%) —
near-universal, real, and entirely undocumented. This is the cleanest case
in the whole audit of "the schema should simply be updated to match
reality" — there's no ambiguity or contamination here, just a documentation
gap.

### `reflection` (`wiki/personal/reflections/*.md`, 24 files)

Already well-matched: 100% on `type`/`title`/`tags`/`created`, 96% on
`week`/`date` (23/24 — the missing one is `index.md`, `type: index`, not a
real reflection), 83% on `related`. No changes needed here — call this one
validated, not drifted. (Separately, `docs/entity-resolution.md`'s
recommendation to relocate this category under `ideas/reflections/` is a
routing question, not a schema one, and stands independently of this.)

### `idea` (`ideas/*.md`, 12 files) — no documented schema

Real files consistently carry `type`, `name`, `title`, `status: draft`,
`tags`, `created`, `updated`, `_migrated_from`. `docs/entity-resolution.md`
finding #1 already flagged the missing schema and finding #3 flagged the
lack of a promotion path (every file is stuck at `status: draft`). Both are
fixable in the same schema addition — see below.

### `organization` (`organization/**/*.md`, ~105 files) — no real schema

Confirmed at vault scale what earlier sampling suggested: real files declare
`type: concept` (the overwhelming majority), `type: organization` (2 files),
or even `type: person`/`source`/`procedure` (a handful) — `organization/` is
a directory, not a type. Field usage otherwise mirrors `concept` almost
exactly (`title`/`name`/`aliases`/`maturity`/`domain`/`related` all present
at similar rates), plus the same `status`/`end-date`/`company`/`workstream`
bleed seen in `concepts/` proper.

## Cross-cutting findings

**The "no `title:` on entities" rule is right for two types and wrong for
two others.** `person` violates it in 7/430 files (1.6% — noise);
`company` violates it in 0/256 (fully compliant). `project` violates it in
220/220 (100%); `concept` in 277/282 (98%). That's not scattered
non-compliance, it's a rule that correctly describes how identity records
(`person`, `company`) are used and incorrectly describes how document-shaped
entities (`project`, `concept`, and by extension `learning-agenda`,
`organization`) are used. A slug-stable `name` is enough identity for a
person or company; a project or concept is closer to a document with a
narrative headline, and real usage has quietly settled on carrying both. The
schema should be corrected to match practice for those types, not the other
way around.

**Cross-type field bleed is real but small.** Person fields on 4 company
files, project-shaped fields (`status`/`end-date`/`company`/`workstream`) on
14–17 concept files and 26–35 assessment/source files. Most of this reads as
migration-script residue (wrong template applied) rather than a deliberate
convention, except the assessment case, which is consistent enough (93–96%)
to just be the real schema.

**Documented-but-unused conventions mirror `entity-model.md`'s Compiled
Truth finding.** §3's `confidence: low|medium|high` field appears in 26
files out of ~2,500 (~1%). Its companion convention — inline provenance tags
like `(observed)`, `(inferred)`, `(reported: ...)` — appears in 8 files
total. Both are well-specified and almost never used, the same "policy on
paper, absent in practice" shape `entity-model.md` already found for
Compiled Truth being empty on most pages. A convention that requires
remembering to hand-annotate uncertain facts during normal writing doesn't
survive contact with actual note-taking; it needs to be prompted for at a
specific moment (synthesis time) or it won't happen.

**Tagging has genuinely improved since the pre-migration vault.**
`planning/vault-refactoring-recommendations.md` (the pre-migration analysis,
dated 2026-02-16) found only 7% of the old vault's files had a `tags:`
field at all. A 1,000-file sample of the current vault shows 978 files
(98%) carry the field, with 107 of those (11%) empty. Worth crediting
explicitly — the migration fixed the biggest problem that earlier audit
flagged — while noting the remaining 11% empty-tags gap as the next
increment, not a new problem.

**Casing and naming duplicates are small but should be cleaned up
mechanically**: `end-date` / `end_date` / `start_date` (dash vs.
underscore), `linkedin` / `linkedin-link`, `author` / `authors`, `link` /
`url`, `type: source` / `type: "source"` (unquoted vs. quoted — same value,
inconsistent style). None of these are ambiguous to a reader; they're the
kind of thing a linter catches in one pass rather than something that needs
new policy.

## Proposed conventions per entity type

Changes are additions or corrections grounded in the counts above, not new
invention. Fields marked **NEW** aren't new to the vault — they're already
in real use and being added to the documentation to match.

```yaml

`source` is deliberately not given one more field-bloated block. Instead,
extend the existing `sources/messages/**` email-thread precedent with two or
three more origin-keyed sub-schemas (article/clipping, Readwise book
highlight, recording/transcript), each declaring only the fields real files
of that origin actually use, rather than growing one flat schema toward 20+
optional fields.

## Recommendations

1. **Document the four types with the largest gap between real usage and
   written schema first**: `assessment` (93–96% real usage of 4 undocumented
   fields, zero ambiguity), `meeting` (`status: raw|synthesized` directly
   closes an open question from `docs/entity-resolution.md`), `idea`, and
   `organization`. These are the highest-value, lowest-risk fixes — no
   migration, just writing down what's already true.
2. **Correct the `title:` rule for `project`/`concept`/`learning-agenda`**
   rather than continuing to flag 100%/98% of files as non-compliant with a
   rule that doesn't fit those types.
3. **Split `source`'s schema by origin**, extending the one precedent that
   already exists (email-thread), instead of leaving one flat 5-field schema
   against 20+ real fields.
4. **Don't chase every low-n field into the schema.** The 9-file RACI
   cluster on `project`, the 8-file `kindle-sync` field — real, but narrow
   enough to leave as tolerated free-form extensions rather than vault-wide
   convention, per this project's own "does this clearly improve" bar.
5. **Treat `confidence:` and inline provenance tags as a prompted step, not
   a writing-time convention.** At ~1% and ~0.3% real usage respectively
   despite being fully specified, the fix isn't clearer documentation — it's
   moving the ask to a moment where it's cheap to answer (see below).

## Implications for `wakil`

`wakil` already stores frontmatter as an opaque blob
(`Note.frontmatter_json`, `src/wakil/storage/schema.py:70`), parsed via
`python-frontmatter` in `src/wakil/knowledge/markdown.py`. That's the right
call given how wide the real drift documented above is — a strict per-type
Pydantic model would reject a large fraction of this vault's actual files.
Two concrete, checked-not-assumed follow-ups:

- **`wakil` is already contributing to this drift.** `_build_raw_file` in
  `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py` (~line 300) hardcodes
  `type: source`, `source_type:`, `origin:`, `title:`, `retrieved:` when
  writing a new raw capture. The target vault's own `source` schema uses
  `captured:`, not `retrieved:`, for the same concept, and has no
  `source_type:` field at all. `wakil` should read a target vault's
  `schema.md` (or a config derived from it) for field names rather than
  hardcoding one vault's conventions into `ingest_service.py` — the
  `retrieved`/`captured` mismatch is a direct, fixable instance of exactly
  the kind of drift this document catalogues, introduced by the tool meant
  to prevent it.
- **`confidence:` and provenance annotations belong in the promotion step,
  not the capture step.** `docs/entity-model.md`'s proposed `wakil entity
  compile <slug>` command (Compiled Truth synthesis) is the natural place to
  ask "confidence for this claim?" as a cheap inline prompt during the
  diff-confirm flow — matching where the two real users of `confidence:` in
  this vault actually set it (on synthesized pages, at write time) rather
  than expecting it to be added retroactively, which the ~1% usage rate
  shows doesn't happen.

That confirms it: only the container file (`00-readme.md`) has a `course:` field distinct from `domain:`; leaf topic files conflate the two. Here's what I found on both questions.

## Learning-agenda as "learned knowledge"

I don't think it's a third leaf alongside consumed/produced. Every individual topic note in `learning-agendas/` is, epistemically, the same thing as a `concept` file: a distillation of external material (a Coursera course, a review curriculum) into your own notes — same provenance test, same answer. What's different isn't *what kind of knowledge it is*, it's *how it's organized*: a deliberate, sequenced program instead of an ad hoc note. That's a structural property, not an epistemic one.

The vault data actually makes this precise, and points at a resolution that doesn't require inventing anything new:

- `learning-agendas/ai-engineering-topic-review/` (11 clean `day-NN-topic/` folders) and `learning-agendas/machine-learning/` (a full migrated Coursera course, numbered by module, with an `assignments/` subfolder holding actual code) both have the same two-level shape: **a curriculum container + topic leaves.** The container isn't hypothetical — `machine-learning/00-readme.md` exists and plays exactly that role (it even has its own `course: coursera-machine-learning` field, distinct from `domain: machine-learning`, that no leaf file carries).
- The container has an owner, a scope, and an implicit completion state ("am I done with this course?") — that's `docs/entity-resolution.md`'s existing **project** test (owned, dated, has an end-state), not the concept test.
- Each leaf is timeless and reusable independent of which course taught it to you (once you've learned gradient descent, that note doesn't stop being true if you forget where you learned it) — that's the **concept** test.

So "learned knowledge" isn't a new category — it's the existing concept/project split applied recursively: the curriculum is a project whose deliverable is your own mastery; each topic inside it is a concept. That's consistent with the KM literature too — Zettelkasten doesn't have a "course" note type, it handles curricula the same way (an index/MOC note linking out to ordinary literature/permanent notes); instructional design's container/learning-object split is the same two layers, just different names.

**Recommendation, cheap tier:** stop conflating `domain:` (broad subject) with the curriculum identity — give the container file `type: project` (`workstream: personal-learning`, `status: active|completed`), and document `learning-agenda` explicitly as *concept's schema plus one field* (`curriculum:`, pointing at the container) rather than an undocumented parallel copy. **Expensive tier, flagged not executed:** retyping the 151 existing leaf files from `type: learning-agenda` to `type: concept` — real migration cost, sequence it last, same as the reflections move.

## Title policy

I need to correct something from the earlier whitepaper. I'd assumed `title:`'s near-100% presence on `project`/`concept` was migration debris — but checking non-migrated files kills that: **7 of 7 `project` files created after the migration (no `_migrated_from`) still carry `title:`.** It's live, ongoing practice, not legacy noise.

But it's also mostly *mechanical*, not authored: `concepts/subsets.md` has `name: Subsets` / `title: 'Subsets'` — identical content, just re-cased. And `projects/1nsp/...md` shows the mechanism breaking on an edge case: `name: "1NSP Second Floor Amenity Renovation"` → `title: "1nsp Second Floor Amenity Renovation"` — a naive title-caser that doesn't know "1NSP" is an acronym. Meanwhile the one case where `title` clearly carries real authored value — `00-readme.md`, `name: README` / `title: 'Chapter 0: Readme'` — is exactly the case a mechanical transform *can't* produce.

That reframes the right policy. The original rule's mechanism (`name` for entities, `title` for documents) is sound — the bug is the two-way classification, which is actually three-way once you look at what each type's fields do:

| Category | Types | Convention | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Identity** | person, company | `name` only | The name *is* the display label; a separate title would only restate it (confirmed: 0% company, 1.6% person violate this) |
| **Document** | meeting, source, reflection, journal | `title` only, no `name` | No stable proper-noun identity to protect — the filename is date/content-derived already |
| **Hybrid** | concept, project, organization, idea, learning-agenda | both | Needs a stable slug for wikilink integrity **and** benefits from an editable headline that can diverge from it without breaking every inbound link |

That third row is the fix — not "make an exception for project/concept," but "recognize these types were misclassified as pure identity records when they're actually hybrid." It also settles `organization`/`idea`/`learning-agenda` the same way without a separate argument, since the same name+title pattern already shows up in their real files.

I'll fold both of these into `docs/entity-metadata.md` now — replacing the earlier "just permit title" fix with the three-way policy, and rewriting the `learning-agenda` schema as an explicit concept subtype with a container/leaf split.

**The "no `title:` on entities" rule isn't wrong, it's misclassified.**
`person` violates it in 7/430 files (1.6% — noise); `company` violates it in
0/256 (fully compliant). `project` violates it in 220/220 (100%); `concept`
in 277/282 (98%). The first instinct — treat `project`/`concept` as
exceptions to "entities use name, documents use title" — doesn't survive
checking whether `title:` is even real content. Sampled side by side,
`name`/`title` are usually the same string mechanically re-cased
(`concepts/subsets.md`: `name: Subsets` / `title: 'Subsets'`), and the
mechanism shows through where it breaks: `projects/1nsp/...md` has `name:
"1NSP Second Floor Amenity Renovation"` next to `title: "1nsp Second Floor
Amenity Renovation"` — a naive title-caser that doesn't know "1NSP" is an
acronym. That could read as "just delete the redundant field" — except
`title:` is confirmed *live* practice, not migration debris (checked: all 7
non-migrated `project` files, created after the migration with no
`_migrated_from`, still carry it), and it's exactly the field that carries
real, non-mechanical authored content when someone bothers to write one —
`learning-agendas/machine-learning/00-readme.md` has `name: README` next to
`title: 'Chapter 0: Readme'`, information no case-transform of `name` could
produce.

That reframes the fix. The rule's *mechanism* is right — a stable,
slug-derived `name` for identity and linking, a freely-editable `title` for
display — the bug is that it only recognizes two categories when there are
three:

| Category | Types | Convention | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Identity | `person`, `company` | `name` only | The name *is* the display label; a separate title only restates it |
| Document | `meeting`, `source`, `reflection`, `journal` | `title` only, no `name` | No proper-noun identity to protect — the filename is already date/content-derived |
| Hybrid | `concept`, `project`, `organization`, `idea`, `learning-agenda` | both | Needs a stable slug for wikilink integrity **and** benefits from a headline that can be rewritten without breaking every inbound link — `name` and `title` are allowed to start identical and diverge |

Every sampled type lines up with one row: `meeting`/`source`/`reflection`/
`journal` frontmatter never carries a `name:` field at all in the census
above, which independently confirms the "document" row rather than just
asserting it.

"commit in change sets", or similar. Default to this behavior whenever committing.

## Procedure

1. **Survey the changes.** Run these in parallel:
   - `git status --porcelain=v1` — see staged, unstaged, and untracked files.
   - `git diff` and `git diff --staged` — understand *what* changed, not just which files.
   - `git log --oneline -10` — match the repo's existing message style/scopes.
   - `git branch --show-current` — if on the default branch (`main`/`master`) and the
     user has not said to commit there, branch first or ask.

2. **Group into logical change sets.** Each commit should be one coherent, reviewable
   unit — a single concern that leaves the tree in a working state. Split by intent, not
   by file. Guidelines:
   - One feature, fix, refactor, or doc change per commit.
   - Keep production code and its tests together when they form one change.
   - Separate unrelated concerns even if they touch the same file (use `git add -p` to
     stage hunks selectively when needed).
   - Put pure formatting/lint noise in its own commit, apart from behavioral changes.
   - Order commits so each one builds/passes on its own where practical.
   - If everything is genuinely one concern, a single commit is correct — don't
     manufacture splits.

3. **Confirm the plan.** Briefly list the proposed commits (message + files) and let the
   user adjust before committing, unless they've said to just do it.

4. **Stage and commit each set.** For each change set: stage exactly its files/hunks
   (`git add <paths>` or `git add -p`), then commit. Verify with `git status` between
   commits that you're only including the intended files. Never `git add -A` blindly when
   splitting.

5. **Report.** Show the resulting `git log --oneline` for the new commits.

## Message format

```
<emoji> <type>(<optional scope>): <description>

<optional body>

<optional footer>
```

- **Conventional Commits** types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `perf`,
  `test`, `build`, `ci`, `chore`, `revert`. Use a scope when it adds clarity, e.g.
  `feat(gates):`.
- **Description**: imperative mood, lowercase, no trailing period, ≤ ~72 chars on the
  subject line.
- **Breaking changes**: append `!` after the type/scope (`feat(api)!:`) and/or a
  `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer.
- **Body** (optional): explain *why*, wrapped at ~72 cols. Add it when the change isn't
  self-explanatory.
- Respect any repo conventions found in `git log` (e.g. an issue/ticket ID footer this

| --- | --- | --- |
| `feat` | ✨ | new feature |
| `fix` | 🐛 | bug fix |
| `docs` | 📝 | documentation |

| `chore` | 🔧 | tooling / config / misc |

Other useful ones: 🚀 deploy, 🔒️ security fix, ➕ add dependency, ➖ remove dependency,
🚚 move/rename files, 🔥 remove code/files, 🚧 work in progress.

### Examples

```

🐛 fix(payout): cap reimbursement at the policy limit
📝 docs: add "how to run" section to README
♻️ refactor(gates): extract coverage check into pure helper

- Do **not** push unless the user asks.
- Do **not** add `Co-Authored-By` or tool attribution unless the user/repo requires it.
- Commit only what the user intends — surface unexpected files (build artifacts,
  secrets, large blobs) instead of silently committing them.
- Keep each commit green: don't split such that an intermediate commit breaks the build
